archetype.name: Pocket Passer (rhythm distributor)
archetype.definition: A timing-based passer who wins from the pocket by getting the ball to the right man in the 10-to-20-yard window, who adds nothing with his legs and is only as clean as the protection in front of him.

report.headline: A top-ten passer whose last three weeks turned cautious, sack-prone and turnover-heavy
report.take:
Goff is what he has been for most of a decade: a pocket passer who wins with timing, accuracy into the intermediate window and a strong supporting cast, not with his legs (20 carries for 23 yards). For nine games the results put him near the top of the league again. His 0.198 EPA per dropback ranks 7th of 54, his 8.47 adjusted net yards per dropback is almost two yards above the qualifier average, and Detroit's passing offense ranks 5th. That sits between his 2025 (0.157 EPA per play) and his 2024 peak (0.293). It is a real season, not a fluke built on one hot split.

The engine is the middle of the field at depth. On throws of 10 to 19 air yards he is at 0.561 EPA per attempt with a 60% success rate, and his 25 deep shots return 0.717. Those tenPlus throws produced 58.9 EPA, against 27.7 from everything under 10 yards. He has also leaned into it: his aggressiveness is up 3.3 points on last year and his time to throw is up 0.12 seconds. LaPorta (0.463 EPA per target) and Jameson Williams (0.424) are where the efficiency lives. St. Brown (91 targets) is where the volume lives.

The last three games are the problem the 3-0 record hides. Over that stretch his EPA per dropback fell to 0.009, his sack rate rose to 10%, and all four of his interceptions arrived. The aggressiveness that drove his season disappeared: 4% tight-window throws against Minnesota, 0% at Miami, 6.5% against New England. Minnesota is the league's top defense, but Miami and New England rank 26th and 24th, so the opponents are not the whole explanation. He was pressured on 31% and 27.6% of dropbacks in the first two of those games, and he looked like a quarterback taking the checkdown and still getting hit. Third down was already his weak spot: -0.113 EPA, a -11.1 CPOE and nine of his sacks.

The interceptions are less alarming than they look. Goff threw 12 picks in three different seasons, so a 1.3% rate was always flattering, and the recent spike is partly a correction. The part worth watching is the drop in aggressiveness combined with the sacks, because that is how a passer with this skill set slides from top-seven to league-average. Week 10 helped some: 303 yards and three touchdowns, even with two interceptions. With a center out and a top-two pass defense up next, the recovery gets tested immediately.

strengths.title: Owns the intermediate and deep window
strengths.body: His throws at 10+ air yards carry the season: elite efficiency at 10-19 yards and a strong return on a modest number of deep shots. It comes from timing with LaPorta and Williams over the middle and outside, plus a willingness this year to throw into tighter windows. The skill is sustainable, since his best seasons were built the same way. It depends on him staying willing to pull the trigger, which he wasn't in Weeks 8-9.

strengths.title: Top-ten efficiency, backed by career
strengths.body: His EPA per dropback ranks 7th and his adjusted net yards per dropback is nearly two yards above the qualifier average. This matches his 2017, 2018 and 2022 seasons rather than standing out as an outlier. With a 3rd-ranked offensive success rate around him, the baseline is high.

strengths.title: Efficient tight end and WR2 targets
strengths.body: LaPorta and Jameson Williams each turn targets into roughly twice St. Brown's per-target value. That gives Goff answers when a defense takes away the top receiver. It matters directly this week.

concerns.title: Recent collapse in efficiency and nerve
concerns.body: Over the last three games his EPA per dropback dropped to near zero, his interception rate jumped and his tight-window throws nearly vanished. Two of the three opponents were bottom-ten defenses, so this is not just a schedule effect. The interception spike will likely settle toward his career norm. The loss of aggressiveness is the real tell to track.

concerns.title: Sacks and the price of holding it
concerns.body: His pressure-to-sack rate ranks 27th of 42, worse than most of his career. His time to throw is up on last year, and the sack rate reached 10% over the last three games. Part of this is the cost of hunting intermediate throws. Part of it is protection, and the starting-caliber center is out this week. It is a structural risk, not noise.

concerns.title: Third down is a real weakness
concerns.body: On third down (7.2 yards to go on average) his EPA turns clearly negative, his accuracy falls well below expected and the sacks pile up. Long-yardage dropbacks expose the line and his reluctance to escape. With 85 plays, the sample is large enough to take seriously.

trend.note: He opened with five strong games, including 327 and 412-yard outings in shootouts. Weeks 8-9 then went negative in EPA with almost no aggressive throws, and Week 10's 303 yards and three touchdowns came with two interceptions, a partial rebound at best.

nextGame.headline: Stingy Tampa secondary, but little pass rush and soft deep coverage
nextGame.body:
Tampa Bay has the league's 2nd-best pass defense by EPA. It allows the 3rd-fewest QB fantasy points and very few explosive passes, and its short-area coverage ranks 3rd, which takes away the easy completions Goff leaned on lately. It has also held lead receivers furthest below their norms of any defense, a bad sign for St. Brown. The openings fit Goff's strengths. Tampa ranks 29th in QB hit rate and 24th in sack rate, so he should get the clean pockets he lacked in Weeks 8-9. Its deep EPA allowed is middle-of-the-pack, and second receivers have scored well above their averages against it.

Availability cuts both ways. Detroit's center Cade Mays (66% of snaps) is out, a concern for a passer whose sacks have climbed, though Tampa's weak rush softens it. Tampa's safety Antoine Winfield Jr. (89% of snaps) is questionable with an ankle injury, and linebacker Yaya Diaby is out; a missing Winfield would loosen the deep middle. The biggest swing is Baker Mayfield's foot. If he sits, Tampa's 28th-ranked offense gets worse, Detroit (-6.5) likely builds a lead, and a run-leaning offense keeps Goff's volume modest.

keyMatchups.title: Williams and LaPorta vs. Tampa's coverage
keyMatchups.body: Tampa has smothered WR1s but let WR2s outscore their averages, and it is only middling against deep throws. Goff's best per-target options are exactly the receivers who should see the softer looks. If he throws to them in the 10-plus window, the efficiency can return even if St. Brown is held in check.

keyMatchups.title: Weak rush vs. a shuffled interior
keyMatchups.body: Tampa rarely hits the quarterback, which is the cleanest relief Goff could get after two pressure-heavy games. Detroit's own line ranks only 20th in hit rate allowed and is down its center. If the pocket holds here, the recent sack problem was more about the line than the passer.

keyMatchups.title: Game script and run lean
keyMatchups.body: Detroit already passes less than situations predict, and Tampa's offense struggles to move the ball. A comfortable lead would cap Goff's attempts, as in the recent low-total wins. Shootout volume like early September is unlikely.

nextGame.watch: Whether Goff goes back to throwing into tight intermediate windows behind a clean pocket, or keeps checking down the way he did in Weeks 8-9.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying skills, intermediate accuracy and a deep cast that turns targets into EPA, have held up across his career and should keep him a top-twelve efficiency passer. The 0.198 EPA per dropback will probably settle a bit lower, closer to his 2025 level. Interceptions should run at a career-normal rate, between the clean early weeks and the recent spike, so expect roughly 0.4 to 0.8 a game. Yardage will track game script more than talent: early-season shootouts drove the big totals, while recent wins have come in low-total games with fewer attempts, so 225-265 yards a game is the realistic band.

What is unlikely to fade is the sack exposure. It ties to his longer time to throw and a line that is only average at keeping him clean, so 2.0 to 3.0 sacks a game is the expectation. The upside case is a healthy center and a return to the aggressive throwing of September. The downside case is the cautious, sack-taking version from Weeks 8-9 sticking around.
swingFactors: Return of the center and interior pass protection
Whether his tight-window aggressiveness comes back
Game scripts: shootouts vs. run-heavy leads

confidence.note: Nine games of a stable career profile, but the recent slide mixes opponents, protection and possible caution.
